title: An Adventure of a Lifetime in McCarthy, Alaska – Spencer Harding
content:
When a last-minute window opened in his friend’s schedule, Spencer hopped a flight to McCarthy, the packrafting capital of Alaska. Check out the amazing gallery of scenery and their adventure below…

I originally intended for this article to have trite sentiments about encouraging people to “get on the flight” or “take the trip”, but as we got close to the end of our paddling portion of our trip, Tyler got the worst news: a close friend and packrafting mentor had died in a car accident the night before. He had been in Anchorage on his way to McCarthy for a vacation with his family. Tyler was grief-stricken, but at least we were on the river, where his friend would have wanted him to be.

I didn’t want to start the article like this, but it felt like even a bigger gut punch when I initially wrote it as the ending. Tyler’s friend dying cast a dark cloud over the end of my Alaska trip, and that is fine; grief is incredibly difficult and rarely a welcome guest. It’s not all sunshine and rainbows (although we did see a waterfall rainbow on the trip).

Hold your friends close, tell people you love them, take opportunities when they arise… I don’t know. Fuck.

I’m here for the gallery, and so are you. These words are a bit of a formality these days. I just want to show you how beautiful it was to experience Alaska for the first time, so please look at these photos on the largest screen you can.

Did you know there is an Alaskan scale for bushwhacking? We only got to level 3; it seems it goes to 5. I hope I never experience the far end of the scale.

I hiked a scree field so steep and loose that it left me with a blister I’m still dealing with weeks after. That scree field was laden with fossils galore, nearly every other rock holding a relic from millennia ago. I can’t really imagine a section of hiking I’ve felt more of a love-hate relationship with in all my days.

Past all the alders, we finally touched down on a river with no gauge (just eyeballing it from way up on the pass), no beta other than a friend who sent us a rough GPS line to get there, and no real idea what hazards might have befallen the tributary in the past few weeks. We saw at least one set of recent footprints near the scout for the sole named rapid, Mom’s Spaghetti. I doubt the river sees more than a handful of humans a year.

It was so interesting to conceptualize bush planes as a common facet of adventure planning in Alaska. It is such a common means to start adventures out of McCarthy and then find a creative way to get back via mountain, scree, alpine tundra, rivers, and glaciers alike. I also learned that only certain butane canisters are FAA-approved, as the pilot straps our bear spray to the wings with a Voile strap nonetheless. Oh, the places your Voile strap will go…

I went into this trip with no expectations, literally none. Tyler told me to pack three days of food, my camping gear, and a whitewater kit. Three days of hiking and packrafting after we got dropped off in the alpine by plane? I just tapped my card for the flight. Smooth brain trips can be the best sometimes.

There is a tradition in the McCarthy area: when they cross the Kuskulana bridge, they get out and walk across the bridge with a rock from the roadside. They walk the rock out to the middle of the bridge, decide what things from the other side of this liminal crossing they want to keep out of McCarthy, and figuratively toss those chosen things into the river with the rock. Most people only cross the bridge twice a season; there are some locals who haven’t been across the bridge in years.

I’m glad I got to throw a rock over that bridge, toss part of the outside world aside, and I hope someday I get the immense privilege and opportunity to visit this unimaginably gorgeous corner of Alaska again.
